tr.td: Santa Cruz cemetery, Dili, East Timor (now Timor-Leste), then under Indonesian occupation
Indonesian troops opened fire on a memorial procession for a young man killed two weeks earlier

Catholic Office for Justice, Ecology and Peace: 1991 Dili Massacre

content.p: On the morning of 12 November 1991, Indonesian soldiers walked up to the gates of the Santa Cruz cemetery in Dili, the capital of occupied East Timor, and fired on a crowd that had come to honour a dead young man. Nobody has ever agreed on how many people died. An Indonesian military spokesman first said fewer than 100, and the government then announced "only 19". The International Commission of Jurists put the figure at between 50 and 200, and a Catholic social-justice office in Australia gives 271. What is not in dispute is that a British cameraman inside the cemetery filmed part of what followed, and that the footage was soon shown to audiences abroad.

The killings took place sixteen years after Indonesia invaded the territory. They are remembered in Timor-Leste, which became independent in 2002, as a turning point in how the outside world saw the occupation.

East Timor had been a Portuguese colony. According to the account in EBSCO's research summary, a civil war broke out in the 1970s while Portugal was planning to withdraw, the left-wing Fretilin party declared independence, and Indonesia invaded in 1975, claiming it was fighting communism. The United Nations never sanctioned the move. EBSCO says more than 200,000 East Timorese died in the decades of occupation through fighting, starvation and disease. Democracy Now!, whose host Amy Goodman witnessed the massacre, puts the same figure at 200,000 between 1975 and 1999, about a third of the population.

By 1991 the territory was nominally open to tourists and traders, but Amnesty International reported that the authorities closely watched anyone suspected of passing on information about human rights and that foreign contacts were treated with suspicion. Amnesty said that at least 30 people, and possibly many more, had been killed by security forces in 1990 and early 1991 in apparent extrajudicial executions.

In the autumn of 1991 the East Timorese expected a Portuguese parliamentary delegation, accompanied by twelve journalists, to arrive at the same time as Pieter Kooijmans, the United Nations special rapporteur on torture. Indonesia objected to the Australian journalist Jill Jolliffe being part of the group, and Portugal cancelled the trip. The delegation had been due on 4 November, according to the International Commission of Jurists.

Activists had prepared petitions and banners for the delegation. Nairn later said that army meetings in villages and neighbourhoods had warned people not to speak to the visitors, and that the bishop of East Timor, Bishop Belo, had told him of a threat to kill a person's family "to the seventh generation". Young activists, fearing arrest, took refuge in the compound of Motael church in Dili. The cancellation left them demoralised, EBSCO says, and sharpened the hostility between the young and the occupying forces.

In the early hours of 28 October, according to EBSCO, a group arrived at the church on motorcycles and threw stones. A fight broke out, and police and soldiers then entered the compound with weapons. Eighteen-year-old Sebastiao Gomes Rangel was shot dead. A motorcyclist, Afonso Henriques, also died; EBSCO says he was stabbed, while the Visit East Timor site says he was shot.

The official version was that a fight had broken out between pro-independence activists and "passers-by". Amnesty International reported that witnesses said the passers-by were military intelligence agents who had come to arrest the activists. EBSCO notes that many people suspected the motorcyclists had been sent to force a confrontation. Rangel was buried at Santa Cruz cemetery on 29 October.

On 12 November, two weeks after the funeral, a memorial mass for Rangel was held at Motael between about 6 and 7 a.m. Mourners then walked about two kilometres to the cemetery. Eyewitnesses told Amnesty and the ICJ that the march was disciplined, although some people shouted pro-independence slogans and a Fretilin flag was seen. In Nairn's account, the banners were bed sheets painted with demands that Indonesia leave and the question of why the army had shot at a church. Others joined along the way. The ICJ estimated about 3,000 people at the cemetery; Nairn thought perhaps 5,000.

Security forces lined the route. A scuffle took place on the way. Amnesty's account describes soldiers who ran after the tail of the procession and beat people with truncheons, and marchers who answered by throwing stones. The ICJ noted that the scuffle happened about two kilometres from the cemetery and up to 30 minutes before the shooting. EBSCO says the procession passed near the Hotel Turismo, where Kooijmans was staying, that a clash with the blocking forces followed and that two soldiers were stabbed. The ICJ places a scuffle in which one and possibly two men were stabbed outside a different hotel, the Resende New Inn, and notes that the Indonesian commission's report treated it as the event that set off the shooting. Amnesty also reported that a separate group went to the hotel, found it ringed by security forces and left after a brief demonstration.

According to Amnesty's eyewitnesses, the shooting began five to ten minutes after the crowd arrived at the cemetery, at about 8 a.m. Hundreds of soldiers with M-16 rifles came on foot from one direction while a smaller group, possibly from the paramilitary Police Mobile Brigade, arrived in trucks from another. Eyewitnesses said the foot soldiers formed a line about twelve men abreast at the entrance and fired without warning. Some soldiers were reported to have fired into the air while others aimed at the crowd. Cemetery walls and the density of the crowd made escape difficult, and some people were thought to have been shot in the back as they ran. Amnesty noted that the firing stopped and started several times, which it said suggested a planned, deliberate action.

Nairn and Goodman, the two American journalists, walked to the front of the crowd to stand between the soldiers and the Timorese, hoping that being foreigners would shield people. Nairn said the troops passed through them and fired once they were close to the crowd. Goodman said soldiers threw her to the ground, and that Nairn covered her with his body and was beaten until his skull fractured. They were not killed; soldiers lined up and pointed rifles at their heads, and they kept shouting that they were from America.

The killing did not end at the gates. Max Stahl, filming inside, saw soldiers move through the cemetery picking out wounded people sheltering among the tombs, beating them and gathering them at the back, stripped to the waist with their thumbs tied. The Catholic Office for Justice, Ecology and Peace says people who had not been killed in the first burst were bayoneted and that some who fled to nearby houses were hunted down; that is that organisation's account. In the ICJ report, a New Zealand student, Kamal Bamadhaj, was found on the road, with only his passport left on him. The ICJ said that repeated military stops on the way to hospital, one of them lasting half an hour, may have caused him to bleed to death.

Stahl buried his videocassettes in a fresh grave before troops arrested him. He was held for about nine hours, then went back after dark, dug up the tapes and had them smuggled out of the country. Goodman and Nairn left East Timor within hours and gave their accounts to news organisations from a hospital on Guam.

The footage became part of a documentary, In Cold Blood: The Massacre of East Timor, made by Yorkshire Television. EBSCO says it won the first Amnesty International award. Goodman and Nairn also produced a documentary of their own, Massacre: The Story of East Timor, in 1992. Stahl, who died in 2021 at the age of 66, is credited by the Visit East Timor tourism site with helping the world learn of what had happened in Dili.

The numbers moved quickly. An army spokesman first said fewer than 100 had died. On 14 November the government announced that "only 19" were dead and that 91 had been injured. The military commander for East Timor said the bodies had been buried at once in unmarked graves in a deserted cemetery outside Dili. Amnesty's report dated that day quoted other sources estimating 50 to 180 dead and unconfirmed reports that as many as 14 people had died of wounds in hospital.

The International Commission of Jurists wrote that most sources put the dead at 50 to over 200. It cited an Amnesty list of at least 60 people dead or missing and feared dead, and a fact-finding team of the Bishops' Conference of Indonesia that reported more than 100 killed. The ICJ also recorded unconfirmed reports of between 60 and 80 more people killed on 15 November.

The Catholic Office for Justice, Ecology and Peace says 271 unarmed protesters were killed and that 250 people are still listed as missing. Democracy Now! says at least 270 were killed in its 2021 anniversary report; EBSCO says about 250 killed and 150 wounded. No single count has been established.

From the evening of the massacre, Indonesian officials expressed regret but also blamed the crowd. They described the procession as a riot of 2,000 to 3,000 people and said the troops fired when the mob attacked. The commander of the regional military command, according to Amnesty, said the only order was "To kill or to be killed". Armed Forces Commander General Try Sutrisno said that if there were victims, security forces had been forced to act and that human rights had not been ignored. Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said that the government had neither ordered the killings nor approved of them, and on 26 November said the demonstrators had ignored warning shots and thrown a grenade. The military commander for East Timor, Brigadier General Warouw, suggested the killings came from "a misunderstanding by the soldiers". One account reported by EBSCO had a junior officer shouting "Don't shoot" and being misunderstood as giving the order to fire.

Amnesty said the regional commander's version was inconsistent in almost every respect with independent evidence, noting that all of it showed the killings took place at the cemetery after the procession had ended and not at the hotel. The ICJ said none of the eyewitnesses it interviewed supported the story of a grenade or warning shots.

On 18 November 1991, by Presidential Decree No. 53/1991, Indonesia set up a seven-member National Commission of Inquiry. It issued a nine-page Advance Report on 26 December. The commission concluded that the shooting was not ordered by the government or the armed forces, that the demonstration had shown elements of pre-meditated provocation by Fretilin and was not an orderly and peaceful commemoration, and that soldiers had reacted spontaneously and without command, causing "excessive shooting". It said that a separate group of unorganised security personnel had fired and beaten people too. It also raised the death toll: where the official figure had been 19 dead and 91 wounded, the commission said there were grounds to conclude that about 50 had died and more than 91 had been wounded. It called for action against everyone involved who was suspected of breaking the law.

The ICJ, whose request to enter East Timor had been refused twice, dismissed the commission's findings. It said the commission failed to meet international standards of impartiality, credibility and technical competence, and called its version of events not credible against the testimony it had gathered. It pointed to the commission's use of the official term "Security Disrupter Perpetrators" for independence movements as a sign of bias. At the time of the report, the ICJ said, only two officers had been transferred from their posts, Major General Sintong Panjaitan, the commander of the military command covering East Timor, and Brigadier General Rudy Warouw, and that they had not been dismissed but would have to appear before an Honorary Military Council. It said no other soldier had been arrested or dismissed for firing on unarmed civilians, while many demonstrators had reportedly been detained, tortured and charged with offences. The ICJ called for an independent inquiry under United Nations auspices.

Amnesty had asked for the same on 14 November. It also pressed for the release of anyone held solely for non-violent political activity. According to the Catholic Office for Justice, Ecology and Peace, some people arrested in the days after the shooting were tortured and killed, and the Visit East Timor site says some demonstrators were held until 1999.

Democracy Now! says that even long-standing allies of President Suharto felt compelled to condemn the killings. It reports large marches in Australia, a European Parliament vote for sanctions and the cancellation of a European trade pact, and protests in Indonesia where students were beaten and arrested. It also says the Bush administration kept shipping weapons. The Catholic social-justice office says some governments, Australia's among them, played the events down at first.

East Timorese voted for independence in a United Nations referendum on 30 August 1999, and the country became independent on 20 May 2002. Because most of the victims were young, 12 November is observed there as National Youth Day. A monument stands in Santa Cruz cemetery, which the Catholic Office says is usually covered in flowers on the anniversary.
